reason: 'Under the mirror were five letters.' She then reads six (B, R, O, O, K, N), and they do not spell her name; the count is wrong and the letters do not match Brooklyn.
'She cuts out little sheep shapes with a round cutter.' A round cutter cuts circles, not sheep shapes.
'Wyatt waved his hand near the grill again. Hot.' A small child waving a hand near a hot grill is unsafe and is shown as fine with no correction.
'Grandpa turned him around, so the tag sat at his neck.' Turning the child around does not fix a coat worn backwards; the coat must come off and go back on the right way.

'Then the clouds came. The sun went away. Gabriel touched the slide again. Now it was cold!' A slide heated by the hot sun cools slowly and on a hot day would not turn cold as soon as clouds cover the sun.

'She blew slow puffs. Then she touched the side. "Cold now," she said. The tea had gone from hot to cold.' A few puffs of air cool freshly made hot tea only a little; it takes a long time for tea to become cold.

'He dipped his brush in the red pot... he painted blue over the red frog... The frog turned green!' Red and blue paint mix to make purple, not green (also 'one more dot of red... turned into a little green bug').

'Four, three, two, one. Still four!' Counting down ends on 'one', so this breaks the stated rule that the last number said tells how many; order independence means starting from a different object, not counting in reverse number order.
'She ate slow, and the bowl stayed full.' Eating slowly still empties the bowl, just more slowly; it does not stay full.
'He looked at his hands in the mirror. His shadow waved back at him.' A mirror shows your reflection, not your shadow.
The story says the book can go home and must come back in three weeks, but never says why (so other people can read it too). Theodore also hands the book back instead of borrowing it.

'The sun was hot on the window. John rolled it up. The air inside turned cold.' Closing a car window in the sun does not cool the air; it usually gets hotter unless air conditioning is on. Also 'bigger than ten cars' overstates a truck's size.
'Her fingers still looked dull... They shined in the light.' Scrubbing longer does not make hands shine; you wash for about twenty seconds to remove germs you cannot see.
'The drop followed her finger! ... She led the drop all the way down.' A finger inside a train window cannot move a raindrop on the outside of the glass.
'She shook one and it turned green.' A glow stick has to be bent to snap the glass tube inside before it glows; shaking alone does not turn it on.
'Mom unbuckled her belt and leaned back.' Mom takes off her seat belt in the car on the way to the dentist to reach under a seat, and this is shown as fine; unbuckling in a moving car is unsafe.
'When he blew on a star, it slid away. When he blew again, it slid back.' Blowing on something pushes it away from you; blowing again does not make it slide back.
'The warm sun had touched the wet paint all night.' The sun does not shine at night; the paint dried in the air over time.
'The next day... A tiny green tip was poking out of the dirt. The bean grew in the night!' A planted bean seed usually takes several days to a week or more to sprout above the soil, not one night.
'He tried both eyes. Now he saw two lights.' Looking with both eyes gives one single image of a light, not two; covering one eye also does not make a light look different in the way described.

'Your hands are warm. Warm hands make snow melt.' said about a snowball shrinking while patted with mittens, then 'Drip, drip, drip... His mittens made water!' Mittens keep hand heat in; a patted snowball gets smaller mainly because the snow is pressed tighter, and briefly holding mittens on snow does not make it drip.
'Tomorrow came... A small green sprout stood up out of the dirt!' A bean planted in soil takes about a week (roughly 5-10 days) to sprout above the dirt, not two days.

'Sofia held the pool wall with both hands. Then she kicked her legs... she felt herself slide forward through the water!' You cannot move forward while holding onto the wall. The beginner also swims alone while Dad sits in a beach chair, but a young child learning to swim needs an adult close by in the water.

'He laid it over Mia, very gently.' / 'Then she fell asleep under the blue blanket.' Mama approves a loose blanket laid over a sleeping newborn; safe-sleep guidance says no loose blankets over sleeping infants.
'That is the dough in the bowl. It is rising like a balloon.' (as the source of a bump, bump, bump sound) Rising dough is silent; it does not make bumping sounds.
The story says you can take the book home and bring it back so others can read it, but never says it must be returned by a certain day.
'The cold spoon made his cocoa cool enough for a big sip.' One spoon in the cup barely changes the temperature; blowing and waiting are what cool a hot drink.
'It made a big triangle of colors over the houses.' A rainbow is an arc (curved bow), not a triangle.
'When he stomped his boot, snow fell off the tree.' Stomping on the ground does not shake snow off tree branches; the story presents a false cause and effect.
The story shows borrowing and a take-back day but never says the book must come back so other people can read it too.
'She poured some tea into the small cup... Now it felt cool!' Pouring hot tea into a smaller cup does not make it cool right away; it only cools somewhat faster over time.
'This is a root,' she said. A potato is a tuber, a swollen underground stem, not a root.
'The flame made the paper glow warm and pink, like a little sun.' Paper that lands on an open flame catches fire; it does not just glow safely, and this is shown as harmless and fun.

'He stayed close to grandma and threw small bits of bread. "The ducks like us."' Feeding bread to ducks is shown as fine, but wildlife guidance says bread is poor food for ducks and not to feed it to them.
'Grandpa lit one candle. That candle lit the next candle... The fire walks from one to the next.' Birthday candles do not light each other on their own; each must be lit with a match or lighter.
'Your tap made it move,' said Miss Ada. Tapping blocks on the table cannot make a toy under a shelf slide out; the teacher confirms a false cause.
'A, B... That is how my name starts!' (uncorrected, teacher claps). The name Audrey starts with A-U, not A-B.
'One bench, two swings, three slides.' The playground has only two slides (the hot metal one and the shady one), and Eva's later count says 'two slides', so the first count is wrong.
A sunny, hot bus stop turns windy, rainy, then snowy within minutes. Weather does not go from hot sunshine to falling snow while waiting for one bus; snow needs freezing-cold air.
The story says the book must come back so other kids can read it, but never says it is due back by a certain day; Luke also hands the book over without taking it home.
'That pin tipped. It knocked three more pins. Strike! shouted Grandpa.' A strike means all ten pins fall on the first ball; four pins falling is not a strike.
'Nothing happened. The drum made no sound at all.' A drum with a loose head still makes a sound when hit, just a dull, flat thud; tightening it changes the tone rather than turning sound on.

'The next day, something green peeked out!' Carrot seeds take about one to three weeks to sprout after watering, not one day; also 'They were big and red!' presents carrots as red when garden carrots are usually orange.

'Then the paper turned pink where the lemon had dried.' Lemon juice dries nearly clear and only turns brown when heated; it does not turn pink (squeezed green apple also gives pale juice, not green paint).

'A baby turtle sat next to his pet!' A single turtle does not produce a baby overnight; turtles hatch from eggs after weeks. Dad also approves taking a wild turtle from the pond home as a pet, which is not a safe or proper practice.
'Leon made a small bed for the mouse from a sock.' Presents handling and keeping a wild house mouse found in the food fridge as fine; wild mice carry germs and should not be touched or kept.
'Ten little teeth,' he says. A talking preschooler has about 20 baby teeth, not ten.
'The warm water made it rise,' said Grandma. The yeast makes bread dough rise; warm water only helps the yeast work.
'At home, he would eat one apple. Nine would be left.' Matthew put five apples in the bag, so four would be left.
'The ducks will like this' (feeding bread to ducks shown as good). Bread is bad for ducks, and parks advise against feeding it to them.
'Ten!' said the lady. 'All clean.' A young child has 20 baby teeth, not ten.
'My mouth heard that!' is left uncorrected in a senses story. We hear with our ears, not our mouth.
'The man touched the grill, and the hot dogs got warm.' Touching a grill does not heat food; the hot grill cooks it, and a safety story should not show hands touching a hot grill.
'Lily taps the crayon picture the way Miss Kim showed her. The app closes.' Tapping an app's picture opens it; it does not close it.
'It made a round shape, like a triangle but round.' A triangle has three straight sides and is not round; the coin shape is a circle.

'Yesterday Milo put a bean seed in a cup... Tomorrow morning... A small green tip was poking up.' Bean seeds usually take about a week to poke above the soil, not two days; also 'tomorrow' is misused for a past event in a time-words story.
'He stirred the spot some more. It looked warm and brownish.' Red and yellow mixed make orange; stirring more does not turn it brown.

'Grandpa was blowing up balloons... Then Grandpa let go of the string. The balloon flew up and bumped the ceiling!' A balloon blown up with your breath does not float up; only helium balloons rise on their own.
'Leah wanted cold milk from the freezer.' Milk is kept in the store's refrigerator case, not the freezer.
'The next day, the sun came out... A tiny green leaf was poking up!' Carrot seeds take one to three weeks to sprout, not one day.
The story says the book must be brought back so other kids can read it, but never says it must be returned by a certain day (due date).
'The baby can have cool food,' with Mama smiling and Grandma giving the newborn a spoon. A newborn baby drinks only milk and does not eat food from a bowl or spoon.
'He helped her zip her jacket up tight so the hat would stay.' Zipping a jacket does not hold a hat on the head.
'Asher went to the store with Mama... The lady at the desk stamped the book.' The story sets borrowing and returning by a due date at a store; the fact is that you borrow books from a library.
'Lucas wrote L, then U, then C, then A... Four letters, all by himself.' The name Lucas has five letters (L-U-C-A-S); the story leaves out the S but presents it as his whole name.
'Bennett drank the cold juice... The juice made the hot feeling go away.' Drinking a cold drink does not cool a hand that touched something hot; cooling the hand itself would.
'He held up the wet paper.' Writing with a pencil does not make paper wet; pencil marks are dry.
'Bread needs to rest all night. So do cupcakes.' / 'Later it becomes cupcakes.' Cupcakes are made from a runny batter that is baked right away; they are not made from dough left to rest overnight.
'"One, two," Luca counted. "Mama, Daddy, and the new baby!"' That is three people, not two, and the story never corrects the count.
'He lifted her onto his lap. Now she was taller than the man.' A small child sitting on a seated adult's lap is not taller than a tall man who is standing.
'Four things, Grandma. Four!' The chair holds only three things (the sweater, the scarf and the teddy), and the story never corrects the count.
